chief_complaint: painless hard irregular lump in breast with dimpling of overlying skin
hpi_details: 52F presenting with a 3cm hard, fixed, non-tender right breast mass with skin retraction (peau d'orange) and axillary lymphadenopathy. Core needle biopsy confirms invasive ductal carcinoma.
ideas: She thinks the lump is just a harmless fluid-filled cyst or a deep bruise from bumping her chest against a cabinet.
concerns: She is terrified that the lump is breast cancer and that she will have to undergo a mastectomy like her mother did.
expectations: She hopes to get a breast ultrasound today to inspect the lump and receive reassurance that it is nothing dangerous.

available_results.note: Hormone-receptor and HER2 testing remain pending

clinical_knowledge.topic: Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes multidisciplinary oncologic evaluation - including staging workup, hormone receptor and HER2 testing, and coordinated surgical, medical, and radiation oncology input - adapted to individual patient risk factors and tumor characteristics.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painless hard irregular lump in breast with dimpling of overlying skin

Key HPI features: 52F presenting with a 3cm hard, fixed, non-tender right breast mass with skin retraction (peau d'orange) and axillary lymphadenopathy. Core needle biopsy confirms invasive ductal carcinoma.

Objective/Exam findings: 3cm hard, fixed, non-tender right breast mass with skin retraction (peau d'orange) and palpable axillary lymphadenopathy on exam. Core needle biopsy confirms invasive ductal carcinoma; mammography/ultrasound and hormone receptor/HER2 status pending to guide staging.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Fibroadenoma (benign, mobile, younger patients) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fixed, hard mass with skin dimpling.
management_principles: Complete staging workup (bilateral mammography, breast MRI as indicated, chest/abdomen imaging, and hormone receptor/HER2 testing on the biopsy specimen)
Refer promptly to a multidisciplinary breast oncology team (surgical, medical, and radiation oncology) for treatment planning
Discuss surgical options (lumpectomy with radiation vs. mastectomy) with axillary staging given palpable nodes, and consider neoadjuvant or adjuvant systemic therapy based on receptor status
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast, clinically node-positive (palpable axillary lymphadenopathy) - staging workup and multidisciplinary oncology referral required.

learning_objectives: Recognize red-flag breast exam findings (fixed hard mass, skin dimpling, axillary lymphadenopathy) suggestive of malignancy
Distinguish suspicious findings from benign causes such as fibroadenoma or cyst
Outline the staging workup, including receptor testing, needed before treatment planning
Describe the role of multidisciplinary breast oncology referral and surgical options

teaching.diagnosis: Invasive Ductal Carcinoma of the Breast
teaching.one_liner: The most common type of breast cancer, presenting as a hard, fixed, painless lump often with skin dimpling (peau d'orange) or nipple retraction from tumor infiltration into surrounding tissue.
red_flags: Fixed, hard mass with skin dimpling

must_ask.objective: Onset and how it was found
must_ask.say: When did you first notice the lump, and how did you find it?
Is the lump hard or soft, and does it move when you press it?
Have you noticed any dimpling of the skin, or changes to your nipple?
Have you felt any lumps in your armpit?
Does breast or ovarian cancer run in your family?
What is your biggest worry about this lump?

history.answer: I noticed a hard lump in my right breast about a month ago, and recently the skin over it started dimpling.
I first felt it about a month ago while taking a shower. It hasn't gone away and feels firmer than when I first found it.
It is just a single lump in the upper outer area of my right breast, roughly the size of a walnut. My left breast feels completely normal.
It feels very hard, stony, and uneven, and it seems stuck in place when I try to move it.
It has gradually grown since I first noticed it. My periods stopped two years ago, so it doesn't change with any monthly cycle.
No, it doesn't hurt at all, even when I press firmly on it.
The skin directly over the lump looks puckered and dimpled, kind of like an orange peel. My nipple looks normal and hasn't pulled inward.
No, I haven't noticed any fluid, blood, or discharge coming from either nipple.
Yes, about two weeks ago I felt a small, firm knot in my right armpit as well.
No, I haven't had any fevers or chills, and my breast is not red, warm, or swollen.
I haven't breastfed in over twenty years, and I don't have any nipple cracking or sores.
No, I haven't had any unexplained weight loss, bone pain, chronic cough, or shortness of breath.
No, I have never had an injury to my breasts or any cosmetic procedures done.
I have never had any breast cysts, lumps, biopsies, or radiation therapy to my chest.
I had a routine screening mammogram about three years ago, and they told me it was completely normal.
My first period was at age twelve, and I entered menopause at age fifty. I had two children in my late twenties and breastfed both.
I took birth control pills for a few years in my twenties, but I have never taken hormone replacement therapy after menopause.
My maternal aunt had breast cancer diagnosed in her late fifties. No one else in my immediate family has had breast or ovarian cancer.
My father had high blood pressure, and my mother is in her late seventies and doing well.
I'm terrified that it might be breast cancer, because my mother had to have her whole breast removed and went through awful chemotherapy.
I'm hoping to get an ultrasound done today so you can check the lump and tell me if it's something I need to worry about.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, but no other chronic health conditions.
I had an appendectomy when I was in college, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure. I don't take any over-the-counter medicines or herbal supplements.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes.
I have a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, but that's all.
I work full-time as an accountant, and I live with my husband.
My last menstrual period was two years ago, so there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-nourished woman who appears visibly anxious but in no acute distress.

Right breast shows localized skin dimpling and peau d'orange over the upper outer quadrant with a palpable 3 cm hard, fixed, non-tender irregular mass, accompanied by palpable firm non-tender right axillary lymphadenopathy; left breast and left axilla are normal with no nipple changes or discharge.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy bilaterally.
Symmetric chest expansion without chest wall deformities or tenderness along the ribs and sternum.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields with no wheezing, crackles, or decreased air entry.
Normal first and second heart sounds with regular rhythm and rate, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended without palpable hepatosplenomegaly or masses.
